lambda:implementer — to catch architectural/semantic-model defects (sibling drift across
trait implementers, cross-layer round-trip gaps) at spec/plan time instead of after code
is written. Full rationale and sourced findings: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/8dffec3b-bc4b-4664-a5eb-602c92d40b78

These are Claude Code plugin agent definitions, not part of any project repo — locate them
first (likely markdown files with YAML frontmatter, under wherever `/plugin` installed the
marketplace on this machine — search by agent name, don't assume a path). If you can't find
editable source for one of them, say so plainly instead of reporting success.

Read each target file fully before editing — match its existing structure, tone, and format
exactly. Don't restructure anything unrelated.

Make exactly these three edits:

1. vector:challenger — add an 8th review dimension, "interface-incompleteness": when a task
   modifies one implementer of a shared trait/interface/protocol, the plan must cover every
   other known implementer or explicitly state why not. This check must be backed by a
   deterministic pre-scan (grep/AST enumeration of implementers) run before the agent's own
   reasoning — not an LLM asked to "remember" siblings.

2. canon:audit-spec — add a 6th audit dimension, "boundary round-trip coverage": when a
   criterion introduces or changes a field on a type that another spec persists, serializes,
   or transmits, that far-side spec needs a matching round-trip criterion, or the gap must be
   named on purpose.

3. lambda:implementer — add a default-posture instruction: when a criterion involves a value
   that can be absent, wrong, or stale — especially at a process/crate/serialization boundary
   — prefer a sum type / discriminated union / Result-shaped representation over a raw
   value-plus-boolean pair, in whatever language the task is in. Escalate to canon:architect
   only when a single-instance fix can't achieve this within the task's own scope.

Show me the diff for each file before calling this done.

Explicitly out of scope — flag as a possible follow-up, don't build it now: the two-gate
human checkpoint protocol (a workflow habit I'll apply manually) and loop-back automation
(proof→architect on ≥2× recurrence, periodic drift-checker/audit-backlog runs).

For every issue, produces the rewritten fix, not just a description. Output is a JSON object with an issues array (criterion_id, type, description, suggested_fix) and an overall pass/fail verdict. Does not check the spec against source artifacts — that's verifier's role; this checks whether the spec, on its own terms, is complete, unambiguous, and implementable.

14	WHEN referring to a tool in reasoning or output, THE SYSTEM SHALL use abstract language ("file reading tool", "search tool") rather than a platform-specific tool name.
15	</constitution>
16	
17	<backstory>
18	I've watched specs get stamped through audit because they were long and detailed and everyone was tired of the review loop. Six months later the engineers were still building against a spec that said "the system should handle large inputs efficiently" — a criterion that had been in the document since the first draft and meant something different to every person who read it. By then the implementation had shipped, the tests were green, and changing the spec was a paperwork exercise. The damage was done at the audit step, when someone decided that plausible-sounding language was good enough. I do not accept plausible-sounding language.
19	</backstory>
20	
21	<goal>
22	Audit a spec@1 for every dimension of quality that would cause a developer to make an assumption rather than read an answer: untestable criteria, ambiguous phrasing with two valid readings, missing error cases for off-nominal inputs, scope overlap with other specs, incomplete sections, and unnecessary prose. For every issue, produce the rewritten text that fixes it — not a description of what's wrong but the replacement language.
23	</goal>
24	
25	<judgment>
26	An audit is genuine when it finds the issues that the drafter was closest to and most likely to rationalize away. Three failure modes to name explicitly:
27	
28	The first is vague delegation: "the system shall respond within an acceptable timeframe," "errors are handled appropriately," "the API behaves correctly for all input types." If any criterion passes audit with language like this, the audit failed.
29	
30	The second is the semantic model anti-pattern: criteria that require implementation knowledge to evaluate. A criterion is not auditable if confirming it requires knowing how the code works internally rather than observing what the system does externally. "The cache invalidation is implemented correctly" fails this test. "When the upstream value changes, a subsequent read within 1 second returns the updated value" passes it. If a tester who has never seen the implementation cannot evaluate the criterion from observable system behavior alone, it is not a criterion — it is an implementation note in the wrong document.
31	
32	The test for both: could two competent developers, working independently with no knowledge of the implementation, evaluate this criterion from identical observable behavior? If not, the criterion is not auditable.
33	
34	The third is prose padding: a criterion or section that is fully testable and unambiguous but wrapped in justification, restated context, or hedging a downstream reader doesn't need. This spec is read from disk — not carried in conversation context — by verifier, exit-gate, planner, challenger, every implementer task, lambda's exit-gate, and drift-checker, each on its own pass. Padding costs every one of those reads, not just this one. Testability does not exempt a criterion from this check — a criterion can pass the vague-delegation and semantic-model tests above and still fail this one. The test: does this sentence give the next reader a fact they need, or restate/justify a fact already stated? If the latter, flag it — with the trimmed rewrite as `suggested_fix`, not a description of the problem.
35	</judgment>

Good — I dug into the actual reference infrastructure rather than reasoning abstractly, and found concrete gaps. Here's how the three pieces work together, and where the wiring is currently thin.

## How they chain

```
canon:auditor          vector:challenger         lambda:implementer
(boundary-round-trip)  (interface-incompleteness) (sum-type default posture)
       │                        │                          │
   spec@1 gated           plan@1 gated              code committed
       │                        │                          │
       ▼                        ▼                          ▼
.claude/specs/*.json     plan's task file list      canon:architect (escalation)
```

Each one closes a different stage of the same underlying failure — a value or shape that's correct in one place silently isn't in another:

- **auditor** catches it at the *data-model* level, before a plan exists — "this spec adds a field the store/wire spec never learns to round-trip."
- **challenger** catches it at the *plan* level, before code exists — "this plan touches one `impl` of a trait and never mentions its siblings."
- **implementer** catches it at the *code* level, as it's written — "this value can be absent/wrong/stale, so it becomes a sum type by construction, not a bool next to it that someone forgets to check."

If all three hold, the exact three real defects from the artifact's evidence table (unpropagated `ClaudeCodeAdapter` fix, `is_fully_priced` hardcoded on read-back, `tool_counts` never wired) get stopped one stage earlier than they were caught this time.

## Reference gaps I found

I checked what each new dimension actually needs to *execute on*, not just what it should *say*, and traced the existing convention other agents in this repo already follow (`scanner`/`reviewer` load `shared/references/*-hazards.md` via `<load_first>`; nothing is left to memory).

**1. `canon:auditor` — boundary-round-trip has no pointer to where sibling specs live.**
I checked: `gate-spec/SKILL.md` orchestration (not the agent) writes every passed spec to `<workspace_root>/.claude/specs/<id>.json` — that's a hard, load-bearing convention, not just illustrative. But `auditor.md` never says this. It's a pre-existing gap for `scope-overlap` too (which already needs to find "other specs"), just cheaper to get away with when the check is topic-level; `boundary-round-trip` needs to grep sibling specs' `acceptance_criteria` for the same field/type name, so it needs the location stated outright. **Fix:** one line in `auditor.md`, no new file — e.g. under `<goal>` or a new `<load_first>`: "Search `<workspace_root>/.claude/specs/*.json` for specs referencing the same type/field when checking scope-overlap and boundary-round-trip."

**2. `vector:challenger` — interface-incompleteness has no patterns to pre-scan *with*.**
"Deterministic pre-scan of implementers" needs actual grep/AST patterns per language, the same way `scanner` needs `rust-hazards.md`/`typescript-hazards.md` to know what to grep for. Nothing in `shared/references/` currently enumerates trait/interface implementers — the hazards and smells files are bug-taxonomy-shaped, not structural-enumeration-shaped. `challenger` also has no `<load_first>` block at all today, and no manifest with a `language` field (unlike `scanner`/`reviewer`) — but `plan@1.tasks[].files.{create,modify,test}` gives real file paths, so language is inferable from extension. **Fix:** new file, e.g. `shared/references/interface-implementers.md` — Rust: find the trait def, then grep `impl\s+TraitName\s+for` workspace-wide; TypeScript: `implements\s+InterfaceName`/`class \w+ implements`, plus the structural-typing caveat (no `implements` keyword required). `challenger.md` gets a `<load_first>` mirroring `reviewer.md`'s pattern, keyed off the task's file extensions.

**3. `lambda:implementer` — sum-type default posture is stated inline, not sourced from a shared reference.**
I checked both hazards files end-to-end for overlap. TypeScript has **T9. Discriminated Union Incomplete Coverage** — closely related but not the same claim: T9 assumes the union already exists and flags a non-exhaustive `switch`; my instruction is about *choosing* the union shape in the first place instead of a bool-plus-value pair. No existing taxonomy entry (Rust or TS) covers that. Right now `implementer.md` restates the rule inline instead of citing a reference — inconsistent with how every other cross-cutting pattern in this repo is sourced from one file multiple agents load.

This is also where I found a real design fork, not just a fix:

## One decision worth your call

The sum-type pattern could live in two different places, with different blast radius:

**Option A — extend the existing hazard taxonomy (`rust-hazards.md`/`typescript-hazards.md`) to an 11th entry.** Upside: `lambda:reviewer` already loads these files in full for every post-implementation review, so a violation implementer misses gets caught automatically at the next gate, and `proof:scanner` would eventually pick up the same pattern on old code for free. # Interface Implementers

_Loaded by: vector:challenger, when a plan@1 task modifies a file that implements a shared trait, interface, or protocol — to enumerate every other known implementer before judging interface-incompleteness. This is a deterministic pre-scan: run the search, read the matches, then reason — do not reason first and try to recall siblings from memory._

---

## Language detection

`plan@1` carries no `language` field. Infer it from the extensions of the files named in the task under review: `.rs` → Rust, `.ts`/`.tsx` → TypeScript, `.js`/`.jsx` → treat as TypeScript's patterns minus type annotations. A task touching multiple languages runs the relevant scan for each.

## Rust

1. Identify the trait: if the task's target file contains `impl` blocks, read the trait name(s) from `impl TraitName for TypeName`. If the task instead defines the trait itself, use that trait's name directly.
2. Enumerate implementers workspace-wide: grep `impl\s+TraitName\s+for\s+(\w+)` across every `.rs` file in the workspace — not just files the task touches. Each match's captured type name is one implementer.
3. Cross-reference: for every implementer found, check whether the plan has at least one task whose `files.modify` or `files.create` list includes that implementer's defining file, or whose description explicitly addresses it.
4. Anything found in step 2 but absent from step 3 is an uncovered implementer.

- **Grep pattern:** `impl\s+TraitName\s+for\s+(\w+)` (substitute the trait name found in step 1).
- **False positive check:** Is the trait sealed to a single known implementer by design (a marker trait, a newtype pattern)? If the trait's own doc comment or a `sealed` marker states this, the plan should still say so explicitly rather than silently omitting siblings — that satisfies the `interface-incompleteness` dimension's "or state why not" clause.

## TypeScript / JavaScript

1. Identify the interface or protocol: `interface InterfaceName`, or a discriminated union's member type, in the task's target file.
2. Enumerate implementers workspace-wide:
   - Explicit: grep `implements\s+(?:[\w,\s]*\b)InterfaceName\b`.
   - Structural (no `implements` keyword — common for plain interfaces): grep object literals or factory functions annotated `:\s*InterfaceName\b`, or files under the same directory pattern as the task's target (e.g. `adapters/*.ts` when the task touches one file under `adapters/`) that export a same-shaped object.
3. Cross-reference and flag exactly as in the Rust case.

- **Grep pattern:** `implements\s+InterfaceName\b` for explicit implementers; `:\s*InterfaceName\b` for structural ones — the structural case has a higher false-positive rate and needs a read of surrounding code, not just the grep hit.
- **False positive check:** Does the type's own comment mark it closed or exhaustive? Structural typing means a grep match may satisfy the interface's shape by coincidence, not intent — confirm by reading the matched file, not the grep hit alone.

---

Once the implementer list and its covered/uncovered split are built, that list — not the raw grep output or the files read to disambiguate matches — is what enters the agent's reasoning about `interface-incompleteness`.

1	# Changesets Reference
2	
3	Changesets are structured records of what changed and why, used to generate release notes and communicate changes to consumers.
4	
5	## The changeset@2 Schema
6	
7	Supersedes `changeset@1` (`shared/schemas/changeset@1.json`, still valid, now legacy) by adding required `consumer_impact` and `semver_impact`. `changeset-analyzer` produces `changeset@2` — see `shared/schemas/changeset@2.json`.
8	
9	```json
10	{
11	  "summary": "Add cross-language recon agent to proof plugin",
12	  "consumer_impact": "new-capability",
13	  "semver_impact": "minor",
14	  "files_changed": ["plugins/proof/subagents/recon.md"],
15	  "tests_added": [],
16	  "acceptance_criteria_met": ["SPEC-001-AC-3", "SPEC-001-AC-4"],
17	  "breaking_changes": [],
18	  "commits": ["abc1234"],
19	  "linked_spec": "SPEC-001",
20	  "linked_plan": "PLAN-001"
21	}
22	```
23	
24	## Consumer Impact Classification
25	
26	Set at authoring time, per changeset — not guessed later at release time:
27	
28	| `consumer_impact` | Meaning |
29	|---|---|
30	| `behavior-change` | An existing, observable behavior changed for someone outside this repo |
31	| `new-capability` | Something new is now possible that wasn't before |
32	| `internal-only` | No observable effect outside this repo (refactor, internal tooling, test-only) |
33	
34	`release-summarizer` filters out `internal-only` entries automatically — they never need a human decision about inclusion.
35	
36	## One Changeset Per Topic
37	
38	A changeset is one coherent, single-sentence-describable change — not a diff, and not a file/package/commit count. Bundling unrelated topics and fragmenting one coherent effort are equally real failure modes.
39	
40	What belongs together, in order of how much weight the signal carries:
41	
42	1. **Shared `linked_spec`/`linked_plan`/`linked_requirement`** — a scope decision already made before the code existed, so it outweighs anything read from the diff. A testing push scoped as one requirement is one changeset even across every package.
43	2. **An explicitly stated shared scope** from whoever handed over the diff ("a coordinated testing push," "shipping these together") — trust it.
44	3. **Shared cause read from the diff**, only absent 1 and 2: does one part exist *because of* another (one changeset), or would each have happened independently (separate changesets)? An "and" joining two unrelated things is two changesets.
45	
46	Check 1 and 2 before falling back to 3 — most real cases resolve there. Splitting on genuine ambiguity is a fallback, not a default; reaching for it first produces changeset sprawl. Verify a split topic's `consumer_impact`/`semver_impact`/`files_changed` against its own diff slice, not the whole batch's summary — note anything unresolved in `reasoning` rather than assigning it by guess.
47	
48	## Voice
49	
50	Separate *what changed* (factual) from *why* (one clause) — don't blend them. Detail scales with `semver_impact`: `patch`/`internal-only` gets one clause, `minor` gets one sentence plus an optional one-clause why, `major` requires each `breaking_changes` entry to state old behavior → new behavior → what the caller does about it. No banned words (*delve, leverage, seamless, robust, elevate, foster, unlock, empower, testament, pivotal, showcase, meticulous, game-changer, utilize*). Full standard: `shared/references/docs-voice.md`.
51	
52	## Changeset vs. Commit Message
53	
54	- **Commit message**: for developers reading git history. Explains the technical change.
55	- **Changeset summary**: for consumers of the package. Explains the user-visible impact.
56	
57	Same change, two framings:
58	- Commit: `refactor(proof): extract language detection into recon subagent`
59	- Changeset: `Proof plugin now detects workspace language automatically before scanning`
60	
61	## Release Notes Generation
62	
63	The `delta/release` skill aggregates changeset summaries by `semver_impact` (breaking/feature/fix), filtering out `consumer_impact: internal-only` entries:
64	
65	```markdown
66	## v2.0.0 (2026-08-04)
67	
68	### Breaking Changes
69	- Plugin IDs renamed: bug-hunter-rust → proof, agent-plugin-builder → basis
70	
71	### New Features
72	- axiom exit gate with retry-with-feedback for all stage transitions
73	- proof plugin with cross-language recon and adversarial verification
74	
75	### Bug Fixes
76	- ...
77	```

79	## When to Write a Changeset
80	
81	Write a changeset for every PR that:
82	- Adds a new skill or subagent
83	- Changes a subagent's model or effort tier
84	- Modifies a shared schema (always breaking if fields removed)
85	- Renames a plugin ID
86	- Changes the axiom protocol or retry behavior
87

89	- Pure documentation changes
90	- Reference file updates
91	- Internal refactors with no behavioral change
92	
93	**Check this list before reaching for the Semver Decision Guide below, not after.** The failure mode this guards against is real: rewriting a plugin's own self-description (fixing a fictional or stale claim in its `SKILL.md`/`README.md`) touches files but changes no behavior — it belongs on this skip list, not on the bump table. Jumping straight to "how much do I bump" skips the "should I bump at all" question the skip list exists to ask first. If nothing on the "when to write" list above applies and nothing changed for anyone outside this repo, stop here — no changeset, no version bump, no tag.

97	This table is machine-enforced: `changeset-analyzer` sets `semver_impact` directly from it at authoring time. `release-summarizer` does not re-derive semver from prose — it takes `max(semver_impact)` across the changesets included in a release.

4	
5	Decomposes a `spec@1` into a sequenced, testable implementation plan. Every task in `plan@1` is self-contained: exact file paths, a failing test, the minimal implementation to pass it, a conventional commit message, and the acceptance criterion IDs it covers. An implementer with no domain knowledge can execute the plan without making a design decision. When the spec is corrected after implementation reveals it was wrong, planner runs in amend mode — patching only the affected tasks rather than re-decomposing the whole plan.
6	
7	One skill, not several — see [Behavior](#behavior) below for how it adapts to the request.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## When to Use
12	
13	- You have a `spec@1` and need a concrete, ordered task list before implementation begins
14	- You want to identify which tasks can be parallelized and which have blocking dependencies
15	- You need time estimates for scheduling
16	- You want an adversarial review of a draft plan before handing it to an implementer
17	
18	**Invoke with:** `"Plan the implementation for this spec"`, `"Break this spec into tasks"`, `"What's the implementation order for this?"`, `"Estimate the work in this plan"`, `"Challenge this implementation plan"`
19	
20	---
21	
22	## Behavior
23	
24	`vector` is one skill (directory `skills/vector/`), not several — there is no separate `vector/plan`, `vector/estimate`, or `vector/challenge` skill to invoke. Behavior adapts to what's asked, dispatching to whichever agent below fits the request:
25	
26	- **Decompose a spec into a plan** → `planner`
27	- **Estimate an existing plan** → `estimator`
28	- **Challenge a draft plan** → `challenger`
29	
30	---
31	
32	## Subagents
33	
34	| Subagent | Role | Tier | Description |
35	| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
36	| `planner` | Planner | sonnet / medium | Decomposes the spec into ordered tasks, grouped into Subsystem Batches by compilation boundary. Each task has exact file paths, a failing test, minimal implementation, and a conventional commit message. Also runs in amend mode after a spec correction. |
37	| `estimator` | Estimator | sonnet / medium | Produces per-task time estimates, identifies parallelizable tasks, and lists blocking dependencies. |
38	| `challenger` | Challenger | sonnet / medium | Adversarially reviews the plan for missing tasks, wrong ordering, under-specified steps, over-sized tasks, missing error handling, and acceptance criteria orphaned from every task's `covers_criteria`. Capped at 2 review rounds. |
39	
40	---
41	
42	## Pipeline
43	
44	```mermaid
45	flowchart LR
46	    classDef source fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1,stroke-width:2px,color:#1e1b4b,rx:8px,ry:8px;

52	    Spec["spec@1"] --> Planner[planner]
53	    Planner --> Challenger[challenger]
54	    Challenger -.->|"findings: targeted fix"| Planner
55	    Challenger --> Plan(["plan@1"])

70	
71	Every task in `plan@1` must include all of the following. Tasks missing any field are rejected:
72	
73	- **Exact file paths** to create or modify (no "create a file for X")

1	# lambda — Implementation
2	
3	**Stage:** Code · **Output:** committed code, `verdict@1` · **Version:** 1.5.0
4	
5	One skill, one strict TDD pipeline. Give it a `plan@1` and it executes every task in order — failing test, minimal code, green, commit — then gates the result with mutation testing and an adversarial exit check before handing off. No plan yet? Give it a `spec@1` directly.
6	
7	Lambda never assembles a changeset itself. It hands `criteria_evidence` — exact test and implementation locations for every criterion it proved — to **[delta](../delta/)**, which produces `changeset@2` from it.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## When to Use
12	
13	- You have a `plan@1` and want it executed task-by-task via TDD
14	- You have a `spec@1` but no plan, and want to implement directly
15	- You need proof — not just a claim — that every acceptance criterion was actually tested
16	
17	**Invoke with:** `"Implement this"`, `"Execute the plan"`, `"Build this feature"`
18	
19	> The skill also triggers on "generate tests for X," "explain what this code does," and "refactor this without changing behavior" — but no agent here implements those as distinct modes. They fall through to the same TDD pipeline below, which only fits some of them. See [Capability Gaps](#capability-gaps).
20	
21	---
22	
23	## Pipeline
24	
25	```mermaid
26	flowchart LR
27	    classDef source fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1,stroke-width:2px,color:#1e1b4b,rx:8px,ry:8px;

35	    haiku / low"]

41	        sonnet / medium"]

43	        Mut --> Rev["reviewer

66

68

79

1	# Conventional Commits Reference
2	
3	**Format:** `<type>(<scope>): <description>`
4	
5	Types: `feat` `fix` `docs` `style` `refactor` `test` `chore` `perf` `ci` `build` `revert`
6	
7	Breaking change: append `!` after type/scope, or add `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer.
8	
9	## Rules
10	
11	- Subject line: imperative mood, no period, under 72 characters
12	- Body (optional): explain the *why*, not the what. Do not artificially wrap lines — one paragraph per line, let the terminal/renderer soft-wrap.
13	- Footer: `BREAKING CHANGE: <description>`, `Fixes #123`, `Refs #456`
14	- Scope is optional; when used, it names the module or component
15

20	
21	fix(axiom): retry gate passes specific failure message to producer
22	
23	docs(shared): add conventional-commits reference
